chapters.title: The Voyage
paragraphs: All that night we were in a great bustle, getting things stowed in their places, with boatload after boatload of the squire’s friends — Mr. Blandly and the like — coming off to wish him a good voyage and a safe return. We never had a night at the Admiral Benbow that gave me half the work, and I was dog-tired when, a little before dawn, the boatswain piped and the crew set to the capstan-bars. Tired as I was — twice as tired, I’d not have left the deck, it was all so new and fascinating to me: the short, sharp orders, the shrill of the whistle, the men hurrying to their places by the dim light of the ship’s lanterns.
“Now, Barbecue, give us a song,” cried one voice.
“The old one,” cried another.
“Aye, aye, mates,” said Long John, who stood by with his crutch under his arm, and struck up at once the tune and words I knew so well:
“Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest—”
And then the whole crew came in on the chorus:
“Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”
And on the third “Ho!” they drove the bars round with a will.

Even at that stirring moment it carried me back to the old Admiral Benbow in a flash, and I seemed to hear the dead captain’s voice joining the chorus. But soon the anchor was up and dripping at the bows, soon the sails began to draw, and the land and the shipping went sliding by on either hand; and before I could lie down for an hour’s sleep, the HISPANIOLA had begun her voyage to the Isle of Treasure.

I shan’t tell the voyage in detail. It went well enough. The ship proved a good one, the crew were capable seamen, and the captain knew his business through and through. But before we made the length of Treasure Island, two or three things happened that have to be set down.

Mr. Arrow, to begin with, turned out even worse than the captain had feared. He had no authority among the men, who did as they liked with him. And that wasn’t the worst, for after a day or two at sea he took to coming on deck with bleared eye, flushed cheeks, a stammering tongue, and every other mark of drink. Time and again he was ordered below in disgrace. Sometimes he fell and cut himself; sometimes he lay all day in his little bunk at the side of the companion; sometimes, for a day or two, he’d be nearly sober and do his work after a fashion.

Meanwhile we could never make out where he got the liquor. That was the ship’s great riddle. Watch him as we might, we couldn’t solve it; and if we asked him to his face, he’d only laugh, if he were drunk, and if he were sober swear solemnly that he never touched anything but water.

He was useless as an officer and a bad example to the men; and plainly, at this rate, he’d soon be the death of himself; so no one was much surprised — nor very sorry — when, one dark night with a heavy sea running, he vanished altogether and was never seen again.
“Overboard!” said the captain. “Well, gentlemen, that spares us the bother of clapping him in irons.”

But there we were, without a mate, and one of the men had of course to be promoted. The boatswain, Job Anderson, was the likeliest aboard, and though he kept his old rank, he served after a fashion as mate. Mr. Trelawney had been to sea, and his knowledge made him useful — he’d often stand a watch himself in easy weather. And the coxswain, Israel Hands, was a careful, crafty, seasoned old hand who could be trusted at a pinch with almost anything.
He was a great crony of Long John Silver’s, and that brings me round to speak of our ship’s cook — Barbecue, as the men called him.

Aboard ship he slung his crutch from a lanyard round his neck, to keep both hands as free as he could. It was a sight to see him jam the foot of the crutch against a bulkhead and, propped there, riding every roll of the ship, get on with his cooking as steady as a man ashore. Stranger still to watch him cross the deck in the heaviest weather. He’d rigged a line or two — “Long John’s earrings,” the men called them — to help him over the widest stretches, and he’d swing himself from hold to hold, now using the crutch, now trailing it by its lanyard, as fast as another man could walk. Even so, some of the men who had sailed with him before were sorry to see him brought so low.

“He’s no common man, is Barbecue,” the coxswain told me. “He was well schooled in his young days, and can talk like a book when he’s a mind to; and brave — why, a lion’s nothing beside Long John! I’ve seen him grapple four men and crack their heads together, and him with no weapon at all.”

The whole crew respected him, and some of them obeyed him. He had a knack of speaking to each man and doing every one some little kindness. To me he was tireless in his kindness, always glad to see me in the galley, which he kept as bright as a new pin, the dishes hung up polished, and his parrot in a cage in one corner.

“Come along, Hawkins,” he’d say, “come and have a yarn with John. There’s nobody more welcome than yourself, my son. Sit you down and hear the news. Here’s Cap’n Flint — I call my parrot Cap’n Flint, after the famous buccaneer — here’s Cap’n Flint foretelling a roaring success to our voyage. Weren’t you, Cap’n?”
And the parrot would rattle off, “Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!” so fast you wondered it didn’t run out of breath, until John dropped his handkerchief over the cage.

“Now that bird,” he’d say, “is maybe two hundred years old, Hawkins — they live pretty near forever, mostly; and if anything’s seen more wickedness, it must be the devil himself. She’s sailed with England — the great Cap’n England, the pirate. She’s been to Madagascar, and Malabar, and Surinam, and Providence, and Portobello. She was there at the fishing-up of the wrecked plate-ships. That’s where she learned ‘Pieces of eight’ — and small wonder, three hundred and fifty thousand of ’em, Hawkins! She was at the boarding of the Viceroy of the Indies, out of Goa, she was; and to look at her you’d take her for a babe. But you’ve smelt powder — haven’t you, Cap’n?”
“Stand by to go about!” the parrot would scream.

“Ah, she’s a handsome craft, she is,” the cook would say, and feed her sugar from his pocket; and then the bird would peck at the bars and swear away past all believing for wickedness. “There,” John would add, “you can’t touch pitch and not be mucked, lad. Here’s my poor old innocent bird swearing blue fire, and none the wiser for it, you may lay to that. She’d swear the same, you might say, before a chaplain.” And John would touch his forelock with that solemn air of his that made me think he was the best of men.

Meanwhile the squire and Captain Smollett were still on distant terms. The squire made no secret of it — he despised the captain. The captain, for his part, never spoke unless spoken to, and then sharp and short and dry, with not a word wasted. He owned, when pushed into a corner, that he seemed to have been wrong about the crew — that some were as smart as he’d wish to see, and all had behaved well enough. As for the ship, he’d taken a downright fancy to her. “She’ll lie a point nearer the wind than a man has any right to ask of his own wedded wife, sir. But,” he’d add, “all I say is, we’re not home yet, and I don’t like the cruise.”
At that the squire would turn away and stump up and down the deck with his chin in the air.
“A trifle more of that man,” he’d say, “and I shall burst.”

We had some heavy weather, which only showed off the qualities of the HISPANIOLA. Every man aboard seemed well content, and they’d have been hard to please otherwise, for it’s my belief no ship’s company was ever so coddled since Noah first put to sea. Double grog on the least excuse; duff on odd days — if the squire heard, say, that it was any man’s birthday; and always a barrel of apples standing open in the waist for anyone to help himself who had a mind.
“Never knew good come of it yet,” the captain said to Dr. Livesey. “Spoil your forecastle hands and you make devils of them. That’s my belief.”
But good did come of the apple barrel, as you’ll hear; for if it hadn’t been for that, we’d have had no warning at all, and might every one of us have died by treachery.
This is how it came about.

We had run up into the trades to get the wind of the island we were bound for — I’m not allowed to be plainer — and now we were running down for it, a sharp lookout kept day and night. By the longest reckoning it was about the last day of our outward run; some time that night, or by noon next day at the latest, we should sight Treasure Island. We were heading south-southwest with a steady breeze on the beam and a quiet sea. The HISPANIOLA rolled along steadily, now and again dipping her bowsprit with a puff of spray. Everything was drawing, high and low; and every soul was in the best of spirits, for we were now so near the end of the first part of our adventure.

Now, just after sundown, with all my work done and my way to my berth before me, it came into my head that I’d like an apple. I ran up on deck. The watch were all forward, looking out for the island; the man at the helm was watching the set of the sail and whistling softly to himself; and that was the only sound, except the swish of the sea against the bows and along the sides.

I climbed right into the apple barrel and found there was scarcely an apple left; but sitting there in the dark, what with the wash of the water and the rocking of the ship, I had either dropped asleep or was just on the edge of it when a heavy man sat down close by with rather a thump. The barrel shook as he leaned his shoulders against it, and I was on the point of jumping up when the man began to speak. It was Silver’s voice; and before I’d heard a dozen words I would not have shown myself for the whole world, but lay there shaking and listening, in the last extreme of fear and curiosity — for from those dozen words I understood that the lives of every honest man aboard hung on me alone.

chapters.title: What I Heard in the Apple-Barrel
paragraphs: “No, not I,” said Silver. “Flint was cap’n; I was quartermaster, on account of my timber leg. The same broadside that took my leg, old Pew lost his sight in. It was a trained surgeon that took it off me — college man and all, Latin by the bucketful and the rest of it; but he was hanged like a dog and dried in the sun with the others, at Corso Castle. Roberts’ men, those were, and it all came of changing the names of their ships — Royal Fortune and such. Now, what a ship’s been christened, christened let her stay, says I. So it was with the Cassandra, that brought us all home safe from Malabar after England took the Viceroy of the Indies; and so it was with the old Walrus, Flint’s ship, that I’ve seen running red with blood and near sinking with the weight of gold.”
“Ah!” cried another voice — the youngest hand aboard, and plainly full of admiration — “Flint was the flower of the flock!”

“Davis was a man too, by all accounts,” said Silver. “I never sailed with him; England first, then Flint — that’s my history; and now here on my own hook, in a manner of speaking. I put by nine hundred from England, and two thousand after Flint. That’s not bad for a hand before the mast — every penny safe in the bank. It’s not the earning that does it now, it’s the saving, you may lay to that. Where’s all of England’s men now? I couldn’t tell you. Where’s Flint’s? Why, most of ’em aboard here, and glad enough to get their duff — some of ’em were begging before that. Old Pew, after he’d lost his sight — and you’d think he’d have known shame — went through twelve hundred pound in a year, like a lord in Parliament. And where’s he now? Dead, and under hatches; but for the two years before that, shiver my timbers, the man was starving! He begged, and he stole, and he cut throats, and starved even so, by the powers!”
“Well, it’s not much use, after all,” said the young seaman.

“It’s no use to fools, you may lay to it — that, nor anything,” cried Silver. “But see here: you’re young, but you’re as smart as paint. I saw that the moment I laid eyes on you, and I’ll talk to you like a man.”

You can imagine how I felt, hearing this abominable old rogue use on another the very same flattering words he had used on me. I think, if I could have, I’d have killed him through the barrel. Meanwhile he ran on, never dreaming he was overheard.

“Here’s the truth of it about gentlemen of fortune. They live rough, and they run the risk of the gallows, but they eat and drink like fighting-cocks, and when a cruise is done they’ve hundreds of pounds in their pockets where other men have hundreds of farthings. Most of it goes on rum and a good spree, and back to sea in their shirts. But that’s not my course. I lay it all by — a little here, a little there, and never too much in any one place, for fear of being suspected. I’m fifty, mark you; once I’m back from this cruise, I set up for a real gentleman. Time enough, says you. Ah, but I’ve lived easy meanwhile — never denied myself anything my heart fancied, slept soft and ate dainty all my days, except when I was at sea. And how did I begin? Before the mast, like you!”
“Well,” said the other, “but the rest of your money’s gone now, isn’t it? You’ll not dare show your face in Bristol after this.”
“Why, where do you suppose it is?” asked Silver, with a jeer.
“At Bristol, in banks and such,” his companion answered.

“It was,” said the cook, “it was, when we weighed anchor. But my old missis has the whole of it by now. And the Spy-glass is sold — lease, goodwill, rigging and all — and the old girl’s gone off to meet me. I’d tell you where, for I trust you, but it’d set the other mates jealous.”
“And can you trust your missis?” asked the other.

“Gentlemen of fortune,” returned the cook, “mostly trust one another precious little, and right they are too, you may lay to it. But I have a way with me, I have. When a mate slips his cable — one that knows me, I mean — he won’t be in the same world as old John for long after. There was some feared Pew, and some feared Flint; but Flint his own self was feared of me. Feared, and proud of it he was. The roughest crew afloat, Flint’s were; the devil himself would have thought twice about shipping with them. Well now, I tell you, I’m no boaster, and you saw for yourself how easy I keep company; but in the days I was quartermaster, ‘lambs’ wasn’t the word for Flint’s old buccaneers. Ah, you can feel safe aboard old John’s ship.”
“Well, I’ll tell you straight,” the lad replied, “I didn’t like the job by half a quarter till I’d had this talk with you, John; but there’s my hand on it now.”
“A brave lad, and smart with it,” said Silver, wringing the boy’s hand so hard the whole barrel shook; “a finer figurehead for a gentleman of fortune I never clapped eyes on.”

By now I had begun to take the meaning of their words. By a “gentleman of fortune” they plainly meant nothing more nor less than a common pirate, and the little scene I’d overheard was the last act in the corrupting of one of the honest hands — perhaps the last one left aboard. But on that point I was soon set at ease, for at a low whistle from Silver a third man strolled up and sat down with them.
“Dick’s straight,” said Silver.

“Oh, I knew Dick was straight,” returned the coxswain, Israel Hands. “He’s no fool, isn’t Dick.” He turned his quid and spat. “But look here,” he went on, “here’s what I want to know, Barbecue — how much longer are we to stand off and on like a blessed bumboat? I’ve had near enough of Cap’n Smollett; he’s bullied me long enough, by thunder! I want to get into that cabin, I do. I want their pickles and their wines and all.”

“Israel,” said Silver, “your head was never worth much, and isn’t now. But you can hear, I reckon; your ears are big enough, anyway. So here’s my word: you’ll berth forward, you’ll live hard, you’ll talk soft, and you’ll keep sober till I give the signal — and you may lay to that, my son.”
“Well, I’m not saying no, am I?” growled the coxswain. “What I’m saying is, when? That’s all I’m asking — when?”

“When! By the powers!” cried Silver. “Well, since you must have it, I’ll tell you when. The very last moment I can stretch it to — that’s when. Here’s a first-rate seaman, Cap’n Smollett, sailing the blessed ship for us. Here’s this squire and doctor with a map and the rest — and where it is, I don’t know, do I? No more do you, says you. Well then, I mean to have this squire and doctor find the stuff for us, and help us get it aboard, by the powers. Then we’ll see. If I could be sure of the lot of you, you sons of double Dutchmen, I’d let Cap’n Smollett sail us halfway home again before I struck.”
“Why, aren’t we all seamen aboard here?” said the lad Dick.

“We’re all forecastle hands, you mean,” snapped Silver. “We can steer a course — but who’s to set one? That’s where all you fine fellows come to grief, first and last. If I had my way, I’d let Cap’n Smollett work us back at least into the trades, so we’d have no blessed miscalculations and a spoonful of water a day. But I know your sort. I’ll settle with the pair of ’em at the island, the minute the money’s aboard — and a pity it is. But there’s no contenting you till you’re drunk. Split my sides, it’s a sick heart I have, sailing with the likes of you!”
“Easy all, Long John,” cried Israel. “Who’s crossing you?”

“Why, how many tall ships, do you think, have I seen boarded and taken? And how many brisk lads strung up to dry in the sun at Execution Dock?” cried Silver. “And all of it from this same hurry, and hurry, and hurry. You hear me? I’ve seen a thing or two at sea, I have. If you’d only lay your course, and a point to windward, you’d ride in carriages, you would. But not you! I know you. You’ll have your skinful of rum tomorrow, and go to the gallows.”

“Everybody knew you for a kind of chaplain, John; but there’s others could hand and steer as well as you,” said Israel. “They liked their bit of fun, they did. They weren’t so stiff and dry; they took their fling, like jolly companions all.”
“So?” says Silver. “And where are they now? Pew was that sort, and he died a beggar. Flint was, and he died of rum at Savannah. Ah, a sweet crew they were, to be sure! Only — where are they?”
“But,” asked Dick, “when we do lay ’em by the heels, what’s to be done with ’em?”

“Now there’s a man after my own heart!” cried the cook in admiration. “That’s what I call business. Well, what’s your notion? Maroon ’em ashore? That would have been England’s way. Or cut ’em down like so much pork? That was Flint’s way, or Billy Bones’s.”
“Billy was the man for that,” said Israel. “‘Dead men don’t bite,’ he’d say. Well, he’s dead himself now; he knows the rights of it now; and if ever a rough hand came to port, it was Billy.”

“Right you are,” said Silver, “rough and ready. But mark me: I’m an easy man — quite the gentleman, says you; but this time it’s serious. Duty’s duty, mates. I vote death. When I’m in Parliament and riding in my coach, I don’t want any of these sea-lawyers turning up at home unlooked-for, like the devil at prayers. Wait, is what I say; but when the time comes — why, let her rip!”
“John,” cries the coxswain, “you’re a man!”

“You’ll say so, Israel, when you’ve seen,” said Silver. “Only one thing I claim — I claim Trelawney. I’ll wring his calf’s head off his shoulders with these two hands. Dick!” he added, breaking off, “just jump up, like a good lad, and fetch me an apple, to wet my pipe.”

You can fancy the terror I was in! I’d have leaped out and run if I’d had the strength, but my limbs and my heart both failed me. I heard Dick begin to get up, and then someone seemed to stop him, and the voice of Hands broke in: “Oh, stow that! Don’t go sucking at that bilge-water, John. Let’s have a go of the rum.”
“Dick,” said Silver, “I’ll trust you. There’s a gauge set on the keg, mind. Here’s the key — fill a pannikin and fetch it up.”
Terrified as I was, I couldn’t help thinking that this must have been how Mr. Arrow came by the strong drink that destroyed him.

Dick was gone only a little while, and while he was away Israel spoke straight into the cook’s ear. It was no more than a word or two I could catch, yet I gathered something of importance; for, besides other scraps to the same purpose, I heard this whole sentence plainly: “Not another man of them will join.” So there were still faithful men aboard.

When Dick came back, the three of them took the pannikin turn and turn about and drank — one “To luck,” another “Here’s to old Flint,” and Silver himself, in a kind of singsong, “Here’s to ourselves, and hold your luff; plenty of prizes and plenty of duff.”

Just then a sort of brightness fell into the barrel, and looking up I saw the moon had risen and was silvering the mizzen-top and shining white on the belly of the foresail; and almost in the same moment the lookout’s voice shouted, “Land ho!”

chapters.title: Council of War
paragraphs: There was a great rush of feet across the deck. I could hear people tumbling up from the cabin and the forecastle; and, slipping out of my barrel in an instant, I dived behind the foresail, doubled back toward the stern, and came out on the open deck just in time to join Hunter and Dr. Livesey in the rush to the weather bow.

There all hands were already gathered. A belt of fog had lifted almost the moment the moon appeared. Away to the southwest we saw two low hills, a couple of miles apart, and rising behind one of them a third, higher hill whose peak was still wrapped in fog. All three looked sharp and conical.

So much I saw, as if in a dream, for I hadn’t yet got over my horrible fright of a minute before. And then I heard Captain Smollett giving orders. The HISPANIOLA was brought a couple of points nearer the wind and now sailed a course that would just clear the island to the east.
“Now then, men,” said the captain, once all was sheeted home, “has any of you ever laid eyes on that land ahead?”
“I have, sir,” said Silver. “I watered there once, aboard a trader I cooked in.”
“The anchorage is on the south, behind a little island, I take it?” asked the captain.

“Yes, sir — Skeleton Island, they call it. It was a great haunt of pirates once, and a hand we had aboard knew all their names for it. That hill to the north they call the Foremast Hill; there’s three in a row running south — fore, main, and mizzen, sir. But the main — the big one, with the cloud on it — they mostly call the Spy-glass, on account of the lookout they kept there while they lay in the anchorage cleaning; for it’s there they careened their ships, sir, begging your pardon.”
“I’ve a chart here,” says Captain Smollett. “Tell me if this is the place.”

Long John’s eyes fairly burned in his head as he took the chart; but one glance at the freshness of the paper told me he was bound for a disappointment. This wasn’t the map we’d found in Billy Bones’s chest, but an exact copy, complete in every particular — names and heights and soundings — save only for the red crosses and the written notes. Sharp as his vexation must have been, Silver had the self-command to hide it.

“Yes, sir,” said he, “this is the spot, right enough, and very prettily drawn out too. Who might have done it, I wonder? The pirates were too ignorant, I reckon. Aye, here it is — ‘Capt. Kidd’s Anchorage’ — the very name my shipmate gave it. There’s a strong current sets along the south, then turns north up the west coast. You did right, sir,” says he, “to haul your wind and keep to windward of the island — leastways if you meant to run in and careen, and there’s no better place for that in these waters.”
“Thank you, my man,” says Captain Smollett. “I’ll ask your help again later. You may go.”

I was struck by the coolness with which John owned to knowing the island, and I confess I was half-frightened when I saw him moving closer to me. He didn’t know, of course, that I’d overheard his council from the apple barrel; and yet by now I had taken such a horror of his cruelty, his double-dealing, and his power that I could scarcely keep from shuddering when he laid his hand on my arm.

“Ah,” says he, “this here’s a sweet spot, this island — a sweet spot for a lad to come ashore on. You’ll bathe, and climb trees, and hunt goats, you will; and you’ll go up those hills as nimble as a goat yourself. Why, it makes me young again. I was near forgetting my timber leg, I was. It’s a fine thing to be young and have your ten toes, you may lay to that. When you’ve a mind to go exploring, you just ask old John, and he’ll put up a snack for you to carry along.”
And with the friendliest clap on my shoulder, he swung himself off forward and went below.

Captain Smollett, the squire, and Dr. Livesey were in talk together on the quarter-deck, and anxious as I was to tell my story, I dared not break in on them openly. While I was still hunting in my mind for some likely excuse, Dr. Livesey called me over. He’d left his pipe below, and being a slave to tobacco, meant to send me for it; but the moment I was near enough to speak without being overheard, I burst out, “Doctor, let me speak. Get the captain and squire down to the cabin, and then send for me on some pretence. I have terrible news.”
The doctor’s face changed a little, but in a moment he had himself in hand again.
“Thank you, Jim,” said he, quite loud, “that was all I wanted to know,” as if he’d put a question to me.

And with that he turned on his heel and went back to the other two. They talked a little among themselves, and though none of them started, or raised his voice, or so much as whistled, it was plain Dr. Livesey had passed on my message; for the next thing I heard was the captain giving an order to Job Anderson, and all hands being piped on deck.

“My lads,” said Captain Smollett, “I’ve a word to say to you. This land we’ve sighted is the place we’ve been making for. Mr. Trelawney — a very open-handed gentleman, as we all know — has just put me a question or two; and since I was able to tell him that every man aboard had done his duty, high and low, as well as I could ever ask, why, he and I and the doctor are going below to the cabin to drink your health and luck, and grog will be served out for you to drink ours. I’ll tell you what I think of it: I think it’s handsome of him. And if you think as I do, you’ll give a good sea-cheer for the gentleman that does it.”
The cheer went up — of course it did; but it rang out so full and hearty that I confess I could hardly believe these same men were plotting for our blood.
“One more cheer for Cap’n Smollett!” cried Long John when the first had died down.
And that one was given with a will too.
On the back of it the three gentlemen went below; and not long after, word came forward that Jim Hawkins was wanted in the cabin.

I found the three of them seated round the table, a bottle of Spanish wine and a dish of raisins before them, the doctor smoking away with his wig in his lap — and that, I knew, was a sign he was upset. The stern window stood open, for it was a warm night, and you could see the moon shining on the ship’s wake behind.
“Now, Hawkins,” said the squire, “you have something to tell us. Out with it.”

I did as I was bid, and as briefly as I could, gave the whole of Silver’s conversation. No one broke in till I’d done, nor did any of the three so much as stir, but they kept their eyes on my face from first to last.
“Jim,” said Dr. Livesey, “take a seat.”

And they sat me down at the table beside them, poured me a glass of wine, heaped my hands with raisins, and all three, one after another and each with a bow, drank to my health, and their service, for my luck and my courage.
“Well, captain,” said the squire, “you had the right of it, and I was wrong. I’m an ass, I own it, and I’m at your orders.”

“No more an ass than I, sir,” returned the captain. “I never knew a crew that meant mischief but showed signs of it beforehand, for any man with an eye in his head to read and act on. But this crew,” he added, “has me beaten.”
“Captain,” said the doctor, “by your leave — that’s Silver’s doing. A very remarkable man.”
“He’d look remarkably well from a yard-arm, sir,” returned the captain. “But this is talk, and talk leads nowhere. I see three or four points, and with Mr. Trelawney’s leave I’ll name them.”
“You, sir, are the captain. Yours is the word,” says Mr. Trelawney, grand as you please.

“First point,” began Mr. Smollett. “We must go on, because we can’t turn back. Give the word to put about and they’d rise on the instant. Second point, we have time on our side — at least till the treasure’s found. Third point, there are faithful hands left. Now, sir, it must come to blows sooner or later; and what I say is, let’s take time by the forelock, as they say, and fall on them some fine day when they least look for it. Can we count, I take it, on your own household men, Mr. Trelawney?”
“As upon myself,” declared the squire.
“Three, then,” reckoned the captain; “and ourselves makes seven, counting Hawkins here. Now, what about the honest hands?”
“Most likely Trelawney’s own men,” said the doctor — “the ones he picked up for himself before he fell in with Silver.”
“No,” said the squire. “Hands was one of mine.”
“I did think I could trust Hands,” the captain added.
“And to think they’re every one of them Englishmen!” the squire broke out. “Sir, I’ve half a mind to blow the ship sky-high.”

“Well, gentlemen,” said the captain, “the best I can offer isn’t much. We must lie low, by your leave, and keep a sharp lookout. It’s hard on a man, I know. It would be pleasanter to come straight to blows. But there’s no help for it till we know our men. Lie low and whistle for a wind — that’s my view.”
“Jim here,” said the doctor, “can help us more than anyone. The men aren’t shy of him, and Jim’s a sharp-eyed lad.”
“Hawkins, I put prodigious faith in you,” added the squire.

This left me feeling pretty desperate, for I felt altogether helpless; and yet, by an odd chain of chances, it really was through me that safety came in the end. Meanwhile, talk as we might, only seven out of twenty-six were men we could count on; and of those seven, one was a boy — so that the grown men on our side stood six against their nineteen.
